analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare hospitals to set safe nurse staffing levels with nurses deciding the ratios.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 36 House cosponsors including 3 Republicans, never received a vote; it sat in the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees for the rest of the 114th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require every hospital that takes Medicare money to write and follow a hospital-wide nurse staffing plan. The plan would be written by a committee where at least 55% of members are bedside registered nurses, not managers, and it would set minimum nurse-to-patient ratios that can be raised but never lowered as conditions change. Hospitals would have to post daily staffing counts for the public, report staffing and patient-outcome data to Medicare, and could face civil fines of up to $10,000 per violation. Nurses would gain the right to refuse assignments that violate the plan or that they are not trained for, and the bill bans hospitals from retaliating against patients or employees who complain.
analysis.who_benefits: Hospital patients, especially the roughly one-third of hospital patients covered by Medicare, and the registered nurses who care for them. The bill's own findings cite research linking better staffing to fewer infections, fewer deaths, and fewer readmissions, and cites an estimate that better staffing could save nearly $3 billion by avoiding millions of extra hospital days.

how_it_helps.text: Each Medicare hospital must implement a staffing plan requiring an appropriate number of registered nurses in every unit on every shift, based on patient characteristics and intensity of care [S2][S3].
A hospital nurse staffing committee, at least 55% of whose members are direct-care registered nurses rather than managers or administrators, writes and reviews the plan [S2][S3].

Hospitals must post daily, in a visible place, the number of licensed and unlicensed nursing staff on duty in each unit, and the data goes up on Medicare's Hospital Compare website so patients can compare hospitals [S3].

Nurses may refuse an assignment that violates the staffing plan or that they are not qualified for, and the bill prohibits hospitals from retaliating against patients or employees who raise complaints, with court remedies including reinstatement and back pay [S3].

The bill's findings cite studies linking higher nurse staffing to lower patient death rates, fewer hospital-acquired infections, and estimated savings near $3 billion from avoided extra stay days and reduced readmissions [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals, which would bear the cost of hiring additional registered nurses. Nursing labor is one of the largest hospital expenses, and the bill gives rural hospitals four years instead of two to comply, an acknowledgment of the strain. Some of the cost could be passed through to insurers and patients in hospital prices, though the bill's findings argue that avoided infections, deaths, and readmissions offset much of it.

drawbacks.text: Hospitals would face significant new labor costs to meet the ratios, and financially struggling or rural hospitals could be hit hardest — the bill itself gives rural hospitals four years rather than two to implement a plan, an implicit acknowledgment of that concern [S3].

Some cost could flow through to insurers, employers, and patients in higher hospital prices if hospitals cannot absorb the added staffing expense; the bill's findings argue the avoided cost of infections, adverse events, and readmissions — estimated in the text at billions of dollars annually — offsets much of this, but the net effect on any given hospital's finances is uncertain [S3].

Civil money penalties are modest — up to $10,000 per knowing violation, higher only for a pattern of violations — so enforcement would depend heavily on the Health and Human Services Secretary's diligence rather than on fines alone [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — patients cared for by enough rested, qualified nurses — is supported by the research the bill cites, and much of the cost is recouped through avoided infections, readmissions, and adverse events. The real drawbacks are unevenly distributed: teaching and safety-net hospitals with tight margins would feel the staffing costs more than well-capitalized chains, and the bill's reliance on committee-written plans rather than fixed national ratios makes outcomes depend on local implementation. On balance the benefits to patients are broad and the costs fall on a concentrated industry that has an incentive to keep staffing lean.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee, then to their Health subcommittees, and neither committee ever acted on it before the 114th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Lois Capps introduced the bill on April 29, 2015, with 10 original cosponsors, and it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and in addition to the Ways and Means Committee [S1][S3][S5].
Within days it was referred to the Health subcommittees of both committees, where it sat with no hearings, no markup, and no vote through the end of the 114th Congress on January 3, 2017 [S5].
It gathered 36 cosponsors, 33 Democrats and 3 Republicans, but never reached the House floor [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospital operators kept full control of nurse staffing levels and avoided the added labor costs the bill would have required; bedside nurses and hospital patients gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hospital operators, not patients or nurses

sides.party_line_note: All 36 cosponsors were House members, 33 Democrats and 3 Republicans — bipartisan sponsorship but overwhelmingly Democratic, and with a Democratic sponsor and no committee action in a Republican-controlled Congress, the bill never moved.

industries.note: The bill would force hospitals to hire more registered nurses, publish daily staffing counts, report quality data, and pay fines for violations — directly targeting the cost savings hospitals get from lean staffing. The bill's findings tie understaffing to infections, deaths, and readmissions that shift costs onto patients and Medicare.

industries.industry: Registered nurses and nurse staffing agencies
industries.note: More hired nurses means more jobs and bargaining leverage for bedside nurses, and the bill gives nurses the right to refuse unsafe assignments without retaliation. Temporary staffing agencies could see increased demand as hospitals fill gaps.
The bill's findings cite roughly $26 billion a year in Medicare readmission costs and billions more from hospital-acquired infections; better staffing would reduce some of that spending.
